newsitem.title: INDIA: Fingers point at pilot error in India air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Fingers point at pilot error in India air disaster.

text.p: Pilot error may have caused the world's deadliest mid-air collision, experts said on Thursday as India defended its flight safety equipment.
India launched an official inquiry, headed by a high court judge, into Tuesday's disaster in which two planes collided near New Delhi, killing all 349 passengers and crew.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who visited the macabre crash site 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi on Wednesday, cautioned against jumping to conclusions.
"Until the report is available, it cannot be said whether it was failure of pilots or the air traffic control," he said.

A Saudi Arabian Airlines jet with 312 people aboard and an incoming KazAir Ilyushin IL-76 freighter carrying 37 collided in flight on Tuesday, seven minutes after the Saudi jumbo had taken off from New Delhi airport.
Authorities said the windscreen of the Kazakh freighter was largely intact after falling some 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) to the ground, indicating it was not a head-on crash.

Aviation experts said only the "black boxes" from the two aircraft, recovered on Wednesday, could give a clear indication of what went wrong. But they said evidence so far pointed to possible pilot error.

"I think it is human error, possibly human error on the part of the pilot, but which pilot is hard to say," said S.S. Sidhu, former secretary-general of the International Civil Aviation Organisation. He said three quarters of all air accidents stemmed from human error.
"It is 100 percent pilot error," said S.S. Panesar, director of flight safety at Indian Airlines. "We do make mistakes sometimes."
Tourism Minister Srikanta Kumar Jena dismissed suggestions that poor safety standards or ageing radar equipment contributed to the crash.
"Our air control equipment and staff are regularly inspected (and) meet international standards," he told Reuters during an official visit to London.

Jena said the Kazakh pilot may have misunderstood instructions from air traffic controllers. "I have been told that the Kazakh pilot was ordered to stay at 15,000 feet (4,575 metres) but continued to descend," he said.
"English was never the strong point of CIS pilots," Sidhu said, referring to the Commonwealth of Independent States.
"I really feel it may have been a communication problem due to language," said a senior official of the Indian Commercial Pilots' Association who asked not to be named.
But KazAir spokesman Salir Mashanlo dismissed language as a likely cause. "The pilot spoke English," he said, referring to the international language of aviation.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant in the Civil Aviation Ministry, said the transcript of the final exchanges between the pilots and ground control showed both understood instructions to maintain altitudes 1,000 feet (300 metres) apart.
The Saudi aircraft reported it was flying at 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) while the Kazakh plane said it was at 15,000 feet (4,575 metres).
In his last recorded words, the Kazakh pilot acknowledged ground control advice that the Saudi plane was directly ahead and 13 nautical miles away.
"What the pilots did after this exchange of conversation is something that can only come out once the black boxes are decoded," Chandra said.
